west-bengal.name: West Bengal
west-bengal.description: West Bengal stretches along India's eastern edge with a cultural and scenic range that few states can match. Its highlights run from Kolkata's lively streets to Darjeeling's quiet hills, the Sundarbans mangroves, and the seaside town of Digha. Visitors driving between these destinations will find well-trodden routes that make cross-state travel surprisingly straightforward.

cities.name: Kolkata
cities.description: Kolkata, once called Calcutta, wears the title City of Joy with ease and is widely regarded as India's cultural capital. Colonial-era buildings, the Howrah Bridge, Victoria Memorial, and its famous street food all shape the city's character. For many travellers reaching by road, Kolkata is both the starting point and the main transit gateway to eastern India.
cities.airport: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport

cities.name: Siliguri
cities.description: Often spelt Shiliguri, this city is the natural doorway to the Northeast and to the Darjeeling hills. It is a fast-moving, busy place where long runs towards Darjeeling, Gangtok, and the Dooars typically start or switch vehicles, which makes it a regular pick-up and drop-off point for cabs.

cities.name: Darjeeling
cities.description: Darjeeling, also written Darjiling, is the region's celebrated hill station, nicknamed the Queen of the Hills. Its tea estates, the heritage Toy Train, and sweeping views of Mount Kanchenjunga draw visitors year after year. Most arrivals come up the winding hill roads from Siliguri, so a driver familiar with the mountain route makes all the difference.

cities.name: Durgapur
cities.description: Durgapur stands among West Bengal's key industrial towns and carries the label Steel City. Large industrial units anchor the local economy, and the city keeps expanding as a commercial centre, a common mid-route halt for travellers driving along the main road towards Kolkata or Asansol.

cities.name: Asansol
cities.description: Asansol ranks as West Bengal's second-largest city and a major industrial centre. Coal mining and steel plants define much of its economy, while its busy railway junction makes it a regular stop for passengers changing trains and continuing by road.

cities.name: Howrah
cities.description: Howrah, spelled Haora in older records, sits directly across the Hooghly from Kolkata and functions as its working twin. The steel arches of Howrah Bridge and the enormous Howrah Junction railway station make it a natural point where rail travellers switch to local cabs for onward journeys.

cities.name: Kharagpur
cities.description: Kharagpur is best known for IIT Kharagpur, one of the country's most respected institutes, and for housing India's longest railway platform. The town is a routine stopover for road travellers moving between Kolkata and the southern districts of the state.

cities.name: Bardhaman
cities.description: Bardhaman, also called Burdwan or Barddhaman, carries a deep sense of history and is well known for its rice economy. Several temples and old monuments dot the town, and it frequently appears as a midway refreshment stop for travellers driving towards the north of the state.

cities.name: Malda
cities.description: Malda district holds the remains of Gaur and Pandua, the two capitals that ruled medieval Bengal, giving the area a deep historical pull. Its mango orchards are just as celebrated, and travellers making the long drive north from Kolkata frequently pause here for the night.

cities.name: Murshidabad
cities.description: Murshidabad once served as Bengal's capital in the Nawab period, and echoes of that era remain in its monuments. The district is dotted with Mughal-era structures that reward a slow visit, and reaching them usually involves local road travel from nearby towns.

cities.name: Cooch Behar
cities.description: Cooch Behar is a town with genuine royal pedigree, best seen at its grand Cooch Behar Palace, which was styled on Buckingham Palace. Beyond the palace, the region blends its own culture with attractive countryside, and most visitors arrive here by road from north Bengal.

cities.name: Jalpaiguri
cities.description: Jalpaiguri is the main doorway to the Dooars, which in turn leads towards Bhutan and India's Northeast. The district's tea estates are famed, and the sanctuaries of Gorumara and Jaldapara sit within easy reach, a stretch that keeps steady wildlife traffic moving.

cities.name: Bankura
cities.description: Bankura is prized for its terracotta craft, the emblematic Bankura horse, and the temple town of Bishnupur within its borders. The whole district reads like an open museum of Bengali art and culture, and the main temples are easily joined up by road in a single day trip.

cities.name: Purulia
cities.description: Purulia stands out for tribal traditions, the energetic Chhau dance, and a rugged kind of scenery. Nature lovers head to the Ajodhya Hills, with Baranti Dam lying below them, and most of these points are reached along scenic country roads from the district town.

cities.name: Midnapore
cities.description: Midnapore is a town steeped in the history of India's freedom movement and serves as the district headquarters. It holds several cultural landmarks worth a brief stop, and its position on major routes makes it a convenient halt for travellers heading down the coast.

cities.name: Digha
cities.description: Digha is West Bengal's best-known beach resort, prized for its broad sandy shore and gentle surf. It remains a favourite short holiday for families from Kolkata, who typically drive down the coastal highway and hire cabs locally for trips to the neighbouring beaches.

cities.name: Sundarbans
cities.description: The Sundarbans forms the planet's largest mangrove forest and carries UNESCO World Heritage status. It shelters the Royal Bengal Tiger, and exploring it means hopping between boats from gateway towns, with the final road legs covered by local cabs.

cities.name: Bishnupur
cities.description: Bishnupur draws visitors for its seventeenth-century terracotta temples, raised by the Malla kings. The finely decorated brickwork shows off the region's artistic skill, and a cab around the temple circuit lets visitors cover the main monuments comfortably in a day.

cities.name: Bolpur Shantiniketan
cities.description: Shantiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore, centres on Visva-Bharati University and a year-round festival of art, music, and the poet's legacy. Its relaxed campus life attracts day-trippers from Kolkata, most of whom arrive by train and use cabs to tour the university grounds.

cities.name: Dooars
cities.description: The Dooars is the access corridor towards Bhutan and the hill states of the Northeast, framed by dense forest, tea estates, and wildlife reserves. Eco-tourists favour the stretch, and the sanctuaries are best toured with a vehicle, since the park gates sit some distance apart.

cities.name: Mandarmani
cities.description: Mandarmani is a coastal resort town on the state's south shore, famous for India's longest beach you can actually drive along. It is a go-to weekend escape from Kolkata, with resorts lining the sand and red crabs scuttling along the tide line.

cities.name: Bakkhali
cities.description: Bakkhali offers a gentle, unhurried seaside escape in South 24 Parganas, well known for its quiet mood. Frasergunj and Henry Island nearby add boat rides and bird-watching, and the whole loop is commonly covered by car over a long weekend.

cities.name: Gangasagar
cities.description: Gangasagar, better known as Sagar Island, ranks among the most sacred pilgrimage sites in the country, lying at the point where the holy Ganga pours into the Bay of Bengal. Its winter mela draws millions for a ritual dip, and reaching the island means a road drive to the ferry point and a short boat crossing.

cities.name: Mayapur
cities.description: Mayapur is the worldwide headquarters of ISKCON and a magnet for devotees from every continent. Rising at the town's heart is the Vedic Planetarium Temple, one of the largest such structures ever undertaken, and most pilgrims come the final distance by cab from the neighbouring railway stations.

cities.name: Nabadwip
cities.description: Nabadwip, recorded as Navadvipa in Sanskrit sources, is the birthplace of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and the wellspring of the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition. It is among Bengal's most important pilgrimage towns, and its temple circuit is usually worked through with a local cab over a day or two.

cities.name: Krishnanagar
cities.description: Krishnanagar heads the Nadia district administration and is admired for its traditional clay sculpture, known as Ghurni art. The Krishnanagar Palace and the Ghurni artists' village are the main draws, and both sit close enough to the town centre for a comfortable cab tour.

cities.name: Diamond Harbour
cities.description: Diamond Harbour lines the banks of the Hooghly in South 24 Parganas and is a classic day outing from Kolkata. Its riverfront views, the ruined Diamond Harbour Fort, and fresh seafood keep day-trippers coming, and the drive down from the city takes only a couple of hours.

cities.name: Haldia
cities.description: Haldia functions as a significant port city and industrial anchor in Purba Medinipur, with petrochemical plants and the Haldia Dock Complex driving its economy. It is one of the state's busiest commercial zones, and business visitors moving between plants here routinely rely on booked cabs.

cities.name: Contai
cities.description: Contai, called Kanthi locally, is a coastal town in Purba Medinipur that funnels travellers towards Digha and Mandarmani. Farming, fishing, and a lively local culture shape everyday life, and it is a handy place to change vehicles for the final stretch to the beach resorts.

cities.name: Tamluk
cities.description: Tamluk, known in antiquity as Tamralipta, counts itself among Bengal's oldest continuously lived-in cities. It once served as a major port under the Mauryan and Gupta empires and now operates as the headquarters of Purba Medinipur, a quiet stopover on the coastal driving route.

cities.name: Alipurduar
cities.description: Alipurduar is the point where the road to Bhutan and the Dooars begins in earnest, doubling as the district headquarters. Forest, tea gardens, and wildlife reserves press close to the town, and travellers heading towards Buxa or the tea belt typically set out from here by cab.

cities.name: Raiganj
cities.description: Raiganj is the administrative seat of Uttar Dinajpur and the gateway to the Raiganj Wildlife Sanctuary, also called Kulik Bird Sanctuary, among Asia's biggest. Birdwatchers and families visiting the sanctuary usually arrange a cab from the town for the short ride to the reserve.

cities.name: Balurghat
cities.description: Balurghat sits as the headquarters of Dakshin Dinajpur, close to the Bangladesh frontier. It matters as a commercial and educational centre for northern West Bengal, and travellers use it as the base town when touring the surrounding border region by road.

cities.name: Baharampur
cities.description: Baharampur, also known as Berhampore, administers Murshidabad district from the banks of the Bhagirathi. Silk weaving, layered history, and easy access to Hazarduari Palace give the town its character, and it acts as the natural hub for exploring the district by cab.

cities.name: Hooghly
cities.description: Hooghly, with Chinsurah as its main town, carries a dense colonial past, having passed through Dutch, Portuguese, and French hands. The district is remembered today for Bandel Church and the Hooghly Imambara, both reachable on a short cab circuit from Chinsurah.

cities.name: Kolkata Airport
cities.description: Kolkata's principal air gateway is the city's airport at Dum Dum, named after Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose and internationally known by the code CCU. It is a frequent first or final stop for travellers, most of whom continue to the city or nearby towns in a booked cab.

cities.name: Salt Lake
cities.description: Salt Lake, officially Bidhannagar, is a carefully planned satellite town just outside central Kolkata. Its grid of sectors houses offices, shopping centres, and homes, and it is a routine pick-up area for cabs serving the IT district and nearby airport traffic.

cities.name: New Town
cities.description: New Town is a fast-growing business and residential area on Kolkata's northeastern edge. With Eco Park, convention centres, and new housing coming up, it has become a steady source of short cab trips to and from the airport and central city.

cities.name: Satragachhi
cities.description: Satragachhi is a key locality in Howrah district, centred on a busy railway junction that offers passengers from South Bengal an alternative way into the region. It links to Kolkata across the Howrah Bridge, and the station area is a common meeting point where arriving passengers pick up cabs.

cities.name: Uluberia
cities.description: Set on the Hooghly in Howrah district, Uluberia is a municipal town whose skyline is shaped by jute mills and industrial units. Its railway station anchors the daily commuter rush, and the town turns up regularly as a midway halt for cabs moving between Kolkata and Kharagpur.

cities.name: Serampore
cities.description: Serampore, also called Srirampur, was once a Danish colonial settlement and is now a favourite half-day excursion from Kolkata. Serampore College, among the oldest colleges in Asia, and the Frederiksnagore church are its best-known sights, all easily toured by taxi along the riverside road.

cities.name: Chandannagar
cities.description: Chandannagar, once known as Chandernagore, preserves a distinctly French chapter of Hooghly district history along the riverfront. Its Strand promenade, surviving colonial architecture, and the celebrated Jagaddhatri Puja make it a rewarding riverside drive from Kolkata.

cities.name: Tarkeshwar
cities.description: Tarkeshwar, also written Tarakeswar, is a Hooghly district pilgrimage town that grew around an ancient Shiva shrine, the Baba Tarkeshwar Temple. Crowds swell during Shivratri and the month of Shravan, and the festival rush is carried by a heavy stream of buses and shared cabs from the station.

cities.name: Kolaghat
cities.description: Kolaghat sits where two major highways meet in East Medinipur and works as a busy crossroads for traffic heading down to the coast. Anyone driving from Kolkata to Digha, Haldia, or Mandarmani is likely to pass through here, and the area is well supplied with roadside stops and cab stands.

cities.name: Bagnan
cities.description: Bagnan is a small Howrah district town on the main highway towards the south. It is a regular turn-off for travellers bound for Kharagpur and the rest of South Bengal, and its markets trade heavily in rice and jute.

cities.name: Arambagh
cities.description: Arambagh is the administrative hub of its subdivision in Hooghly district. It doubles as the pilgrimage base for Kamarpukur, where Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa was born, and the surrounding temple circuit keeps a steady stream of taxi traffic moving along these country roads.

cities.name: Barasat
cities.description: Barasat administers North 24 Parganas, one of the country's most densely populated districts, from just 20 km outside Kolkata. It is a thriving commercial centre and a natural turn-off for traffic heading north towards North Bengal or the Bangladesh border, making it a frequent taxi start and end point.

cities.name: Kalyani
cities.description: A planned satellite township in Nadia district, Kalyani is known well beyond the state for JNMCH and Kalyani University. Patients travel here for treatment from all corners of West Bengal and Bangladesh, and the steady flow of medical visitors arriving by train usually continues by local cab.

cities.name: Bongaon
cities.description: Bongaon sits in North 24 Parganas close to the Bangladesh border and handles a heavy volume of cross-border trade. It is the doorway to the Petrapole–Benapole land crossing, India's busiest, and trucks and passengers moving through here keep local transport in constant demand.

cities.name: Ranaghat
cities.description: Ranaghat is a busy Nadia district city whose railway junction ties together Kolkata, Bongaon, Krishnanagar, and points in North Bengal. Beyond the trains, it has its own share of history and cultural activity, and travellers changing modes here routinely hire cabs for the onward leg.

cities.name: Basirhat
cities.description: Basirhat heads its subdivision in North 24 Parganas, lying near the Bangladesh border beside the Ichhamati River. It is the commercial heart of the border country and a staging point for trips towards the Sundarbans, with most onward travel from the town done by road.

cities.name: Barrackpore
cities.description: In North 24 Parganas, along the Hooghly, stands Barrackpore, a garrison town bound up with India's independence struggle. It was here that Mangal Pandey set off the events of 1857, and today Gandhi Ghat and the Army Museum draw history-minded visitors, most of whom come up by road or train from Kolkata.

cities.name: Dum Dum
cities.description: Dum Dum, on the edge of North 24 Parganas, is best known for lying right next to Kolkata's international airport. Air travellers passing through make it one of the city's busiest transit areas, and its mix of industry and housing keeps a steady stream of cabs moving along its main roads.

cities.name: Habra
cities.description: Habra is a busy market town in North 24 Parganas, set right on the Barasat–Bongaon road. That position makes it a common turning point for travellers heading towards the Sundarbans, Basirhat, or the Bangladesh frontier, and local taxis line up near the market for such runs.

cities.name: Naihati
cities.description: On the Hooghly's west bank in North 24 Parganas, Naihati is a municipal town whose industrial identity came from its jute mills. Its literary fame rests on Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, the author of Pather Panchali, who was born here, and the town is a familiar riverside stop on routes towards the north.

cities.name: Kakdwip
cities.description: Kakdwip is the practical starting point for Sagar Island and one of the more important towns of South 24 Parganas. Its Kachuberia ferry terminal carries pilgrims across to Gangasagar, while the town's fishing community and its closeness to the Sundarbans keep traffic steady on the roads leading in.

cities.name: Jhargram
cities.description: Jhargram heads its district amid dense sal woodland and gentle countryside, marketed simply as a forest retreat. The Jhargram Palace is the centrepiece, tribal culture tourism runs close by, and visitors usually cover the nearby forests and palace grounds with a hired car over a couple of days.

cities.name: Raniganj
cities.description: Raniganj is a coal town with a long pedigree in Paschim Bardhaman, often named the origin point of Indian coal mining. The Raniganj Coalfield, in work since 1774, stays among the country's largest, and the town is a regular stop for industrial travel along the Asansol–Durgapur belt.

cities.name: Kalna
cities.description: Kalna, also called Ambika Kalna, is a temple town in Purba Bardhaman beside the Hooghly. Its Rajbari encloses 108 Shiva temples set out in two concentric rings, an architectural curiosity unique to Bengal, and day-trippers usually book a cab from a nearby town to come and see it.

cities.name: Katwa
cities.description: Katwa is a Purba Bardhaman town of real historical weight, standing where the Bhagirathi and Ajay rivers meet. It claims Nityananda Prabhu as a native and was the setting for the Battle of Katwa in Siraj ud-Daulah's era, and travellers passing along the northern route often pause here for its ghats.

cities.name: Chakdah
cities.description: Chakdah is a Nadia district town recognised for farm produce, sports goods, and a steady flow of traffic between Kolkata and Krishnanagar. It has also earned a reputation for turning out athletes, and its position on the main road makes it an easy brief stop for through travellers.

cities.name: Islampur
cities.description: Islampur is a busy commercial city in Uttar Dinajpur and one of the trade centres of North Bengal. Sitting on the main highway, it serves as the natural entry point for journeys towards Sikkim and Darjeeling, and cabs line up here for the long mountain runs.

cities.name: Dalkhola
cities.description: Dalkhola occupies a strategic position in Uttar Dinajpur, at the point where West Bengal, Bihar, and Jharkhand nearly converge. It is a well-used staging point on the highway for journeys towards North Bengal, Sikkim, and the Northeast, and drivers routinely pull in here for fuel and refreshments.

cities.name: Lalbagh
cities.description: Lalbagh, a Murshidabad district town, is remembered for an unfinished palace begun for Nawab Shaista Khan and one of Aurangzeb's sons, a structure now known as the ruins of Lalbagh Fort. It offers a quiet window into Bengal's Mughal past, and most heritage visitors reach it by road from Murshidabad town.

cities.name: Beldanga
cities.description: Beldanga lies on the Bhagirathi in Murshidabad district, a town whose silk looms are locally famous. Its railway junction links Baharampur with Kolkata and Azimganj, and passengers changing trains here often take a short cab ride into the market area.

cities.name: Karimpur
cities.description: Karimpur is a Nadia district town lying close to the Bangladesh border, known mainly for vegetable farming and busy local trading. It ranks among the district's significant agricultural towns, and its bazaars see constant movement of small commercial vehicles and goods.

odisha.name: Odisha
odisha.description: Odisha hugs India's eastern coastline, where centuries-old temples sit beside tribal villages and quiet beaches. The state's signature stops include the Sun Temple at Konark, the holy town of Puri, and the wildlife reserves of Simlipal. Road travel across this stretch is well served, making it a comfortable drive for first-time visitors.

cities.name: Bhubaneswar
cities.description: Bhubaneswar is Odisha's capital, widely nicknamed the Temple City of India for the seven hundred-plus temples spread across it. Beyond the shrines it has grown into an IT centre and the state's transport hub, where most long-distance travellers switch to cabs for onward trips.

cities.name: Puri
cities.description: Puri ranks among the four sacred Dhams and is inseparable from the Jagannath Temple. Its Golden Beach and the huge annual Rath Yatra bring in millions of pilgrims and holidaymakers, and the roughly hour-long drive from Bhubaneswar is one of the busiest cab routes in the state.

cities.name: Cuttack
cities.description: Cuttack, nicknamed the Silver City, once served as Odisha's capital and is among the country's most ancient cities. It is celebrated for silver filigree craft, the ruins of Barabati Fort, and grand Durga Puja, and sits only a short drive from Bhubaneswar, making it an easy day trip by cab.

cities.name: Rourkela
cities.description: Rourkela is one of Odisha's industrial heavyweights, built around the Rourkela Steel Plant and home to NIT Rourkela. Waterfalls and the Mandira Dam lie within easy reach of town, and visitors driving in from Ranchi or Bhubaneswar find good roads all the way.

cities.name: Sambalpur
cities.description: Sambalpur is identified first with its handwoven Sambalpuri sarees, the enormous Hirakud Dam, and the colourful Sitalsasthi carnival. It sits on the western edge of the state, and travellers heading towards the dam or onward to Jharsuguda usually pass straight through town by road.

cities.name: Berhampur
cities.description: Berhampur, also written Brahmapur, is the principal commercial city of southern Odisha, celebrated for its silk sarees. It also serves as the stepping-off point for Gopalpur-on-Sea, and cabs working the short coastal hop between town and beach are a familiar sight.

cities.name: Balasore
cities.description: Balasore, called Baleshwar locally, is known for Chandipur Beach, whose sea withdraws as far as 5 km at low tide. The district also hosts India's missile testing range, and travellers on the Kolkata–Bhubaneswar highway regularly pause here.

cities.name: Bhadrak
cities.description: Bhadrak stands on the Salandi River in Odisha and works as a commercial centre for the surrounding coastal belt. Its railway junction sits on the busy Howrah–Chennai trunk line, while the Akhandalamani Temple draws steady pilgrims, keeping the station and bus stand areas active with local transport.

cities.name: Konark
cities.description: Konark's fame rests on the Sun Temple, a UNESCO-listed masterwork of Kalinga architecture built in the shape of a colossal chariot in the thirteenth century. Most visitors make it a day trip from Puri, arriving by road along the coastal stretch.

cities.name: Chilika
cities.description: Asia's biggest brackish-water lagoon, Chilika, is a protected Ramsar wetland that turns into a winter roosting ground for enormous flocks of migratory birds. Most visitors drive to the shore and then continue by boat from the nearest landing point.

cities.name: Dhenkanal
cities.description: Dhenkanal is a historic district town with a strong cultural identity and quick access to Kapilash Temple. Forested terrain and the Saptasajya hills offer easy countryside outings, and most of these spots are best reached by car from the town centre.

cities.name: Koraput
cities.description: Koraput stands apart for its rich tribal culture, coffee estates, and hilly scenery. Travellers come for genuine tribal tourism experiences, and getting around the district usually means hiring a cab for the hilly roads between villages and viewpoints.

cities.name: Rayagada
cities.description: Rayagada is the home ground of the Dongariya Kondh people and opens onto the scenic Chatikona Valley. It offers authentic tribal tourism, with most excursions from town requiring a vehicle for the valley roads.

cities.name: Angul
cities.description: Angul is a significant industrial city in Odisha, anchored by the NALCO aluminium smelter and several thermal power plants. Nature lovers use it as the gateway to the Satkosia Gorge wildlife sanctuary, a drive of under an hour from town.

cities.name: Jharsuguda
cities.description: Jharsuguda is an industrial and mining hub in western Odisha, powered by coal mines and electricity plants. Its railway junction ties Odisha to Chhattisgarh, making the town a familiar interchange where long-distance travellers switch to road transport.

cities.name: Baripada
cities.description: Baripada serves as the access point to Simlipal National Park, counted among India's principal tiger reserves. The town itself is known for tribal traditions, its Chhau dance festival, and a celebrated Rath Yatra, and safari-goers typically arrange cabs here for the run to the park gates.

cities.name: Jeypore
cities.description: Jeypore, in Koraput district, opens the door to the tribal heartland of southern Odisha, surrounded by waterfalls and distinct local culture. The Haat Kali Temple and the weekly tribal markets pull most visitors, and these are best covered with a hired car over a few days.

cities.name: Gopalpur
cities.description: Gopalpur-on-Sea is a quiet stretch of coast in southern Odisha, carrying an old-world feel with its colonial lighthouse and calm sands. Once a working port, it now exists purely as a relaxed beach retreat, reached by a short drive from Berhampur.

jharkhand.name: Jharkhand
jharkhand.description: Jharkhand earns its nickname, the Land of Forests, thanks to dense woodlands, cascading waterfalls, and vibrant tribal traditions. Destinations range from Ranchi's waterfall country to sacred Deoghar and the industrial centres of Jamshedpur and Dhanbad. The state's highways connect these far-flung corners, so self-driving itineraries are entirely workable.

cities.name: Ranchi
cities.description: Ranchi, the capital of Jharkhand, wears the title City of Waterfalls thanks to Hundru, Jonha, and Dassam Falls ringing the town. It balances city life with easy nature access, and its position on the state's road network makes it the natural hub where travellers hire cabs for the surrounding falls.

cities.name: Jamshedpur
cities.description: Jamshedpur, called the Steel City, was laid out by the Tata Group as India's first planned industrial town. Green spaces such as Jubilee Park, the Dimna Lake reservoir, and the Tata Steel works anchor its identity, and the city's clean grid layout makes getting around by cab unusually easy.

cities.name: Dhanbad
cities.description: Dhanbad has earned the label Coal Capital of India, with coal mines pressing in from every side. It is also home to IIT ISM, and the city's industrial traffic means booked cabs and taxis are in regular demand around its stations and market roads.

cities.name: Bokaro
cities.description: Bokaro Steel City is built around one of India's biggest steel plants, with a neat layout and generous green spaces. Beyond the plant complex, residents and visitors enjoy City Park and the Jawaharlal Nehru Biological Park, all conveniently linked by local roads.

cities.name: Hazaribagh
cities.description: Called the City of a Thousand Gardens, Hazaribagh earns the name through its lush greenery, the Canary Hill viewpoint, and the Hazaribagh Wildlife Sanctuary. Travellers heading for the sanctuary or the hill often stop in town to arrange a four-wheeler for the forest roads.

cities.name: Deoghar
cities.description: Deoghar is among India's holiest towns, centred on Baidyanath Dham, one of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines. During the Shravani Mela it handles millions of pilgrims, and the huge festival crowds mean a constant stream of buses and taxis around the temple area.

cities.name: Giridih
cities.description: Giridih's claim to fame is Parasnath Hill, the holiest site in Jainism, capped with 24 Jain temples. It draws pilgrims throughout the year, and most visitors make the climb after reaching the hill base by road from town.

cities.name: Ramgarh
cities.description: Ramgarh is a coal-mining town whose best-known sight lies outside it: the Rajrappa Temple, set where the Damodar and Bhairavi rivers meet. Day-trippers from nearby cities usually drive here directly, making it a regular weekend cab route.

cities.name: Palamu
cities.description: Palamu's biggest draw is Betla National Park, also called the Palamu Tiger Reserve, backed by the old Palamu Fort and thick forest. It has become a firm favourite for eco-tourism, with visitors moving between the fort and park gates by road.

cities.name: Netarhat
cities.description: Netarhat, dubbed the Queen of Chotanagpur, is a small hill station prized for dramatic sunrises and sunsets over the sal forests. It is the kind of place reached on a winding mountain road, and drivers here know the hairpin approach well.

cities.name: Betla
cities.description: Betla is essentially defined by its national park, Betla National Park, which was among the earliest tiger reserves created in the country. Tigers, elephants, and a wide range of wildlife live within its boundary, and safari traffic to the park keeps the local roads busy in season.

cities.name: Dumka
cities.description: Dumka serves as Jharkhand's sub-capital and the administrative seat of the Santal Pargana division. Tribal heritage, the Baskinath temple, and the scenic Masanjore Dam give travellers reasons to linger, and the dam makes a pleasant short drive from town.

cities.name: Chaibasa
cities.description: Chaibasa administers the West Singhbhum district and sits close to the deep forests of Saranda. Its tribal communities, iron ore mining, and nearby waterfalls give the town a distinct character, and excursions into the forest are usually organised by cab from here.

cities.name: Sahebganj
cities.description: Sahebganj is a town of old importance on the Ganges, backed by the Rajmahal Hills and known for ancient fossil beds and the Kanhaiya Sthan temple. As a river port it once handled heavy cargo, and today it draws visitors who drive in along the riverside road.

cities.name: Godda
cities.description: Godda is a quiet Jharkhand town, mainly agricultural, with a strong tribal identity and the Rajmahal Hills in view. The Sundarban Dam provides the chief outing, a drive of a short distance from the town centre.

cities.name: Latehar
cities.description: Latehar is the approach town for Netarhat and guards the route to Lodh Falls, the tallest waterfall in Jharkhand. The district's dense forest cover and trail network attract trekkers, and most expeditions start with a drive from Latehar into the hills.

cities.name: Tatanagar
cities.description: Tatanagar functions as a major railway junction and the practical gateway to Jamshedpur. Passengers arriving here regularly complete the last leg into the city by cab.

cities.name: Adityapur
cities.description: Adityapur is an industrial town in Seraikela Kharsawan district, lying almost shoulder to shoulder with Jamshedpur. It handles a large share of the region's manufacturing, and its factories generate steady daily taxi traffic along the connecting road.

cities.name: Khunti
cities.description: The Ulgulan, a revolt against British rule, was led by Birsa Munda, born in Khunti, and the district honours him with the Birsa Munda Memorial Museum, a stop on most itineraries. Around 35 km from Ranchi, it draws visitors interested in tribal heritage, forests, and waterfalls, and the road from the capital keeps it an easy day trip.

cities.name: Gumla
cities.description: Gumla, ringed by forest and waterfalls, is a scenic district town with deep roots in Nagpuri culture and tribal tradition. Its headline sights are the Anjandhaam Temple, a major shrine for Hanuman devotees, and the Nagpheni falls, both reached along pleasant drives from town.

cities.name: Simdega
cities.description: Simdega sits on Jharkhand's southwestern edge along the Odisha border, where most residents belong to tribal communities and the district is gently growing into an eco-tourism destination. Its green forests, including the Keolajhar area, draw nature travellers, while the region's knack for turning out footballers adds local colour.

cities.name: Chatra
cities.description: Chatra is a scenic Jharkhand district of waterfalls and open landscapes, sitting along the old Grand Trunk Road. The Tamas waterfall, also known as Tandwa Falls, and the historic Ituriaghat are the main drawcards, and the old highway makes the district straightforward to reach by road.

cities.name: Lohardaga
cities.description: Lohardaga, 60 km from Ranchi, is a quiet district town on the road towards Netarhat, known for its bauxite reserves and a strong tribal culture. The Koel, the river that runs through town, adds to the scenery, and travellers heading for the hill station frequently stop here to refresh before the climb.

cities.name: Pakur
cities.description: Pakur, on the West Bengal border within the Santhal Pargana division, is a district town defined by stone quarrying and mining. It stands on the Brahmani River, and its substantial Santhal population and heritage make it a culturally interesting stop for travellers passing between the two states.

cities.name: Jamtara
cities.description: Jamtara lies about 150 km from Kolkata, close to the West Bengal border, in a stretch of Jharkhand known for coal country. Its spot on the highway between Asansol and Dhanbad makes it a natural halt for drivers, with fuel stops and roadside eateries lining the route.

cities.name: Koderma
cities.description: Koderma is a Jharkhand district town whose mica deposits have earned it the nickname Mica Capital of the World. It stands on the Grand Trunk Road, midway between Hazaribagh and Gaya, a position that keeps steady traffic passing through and makes it a convenient halt for drivers.

cities.name: Seraikela
cities.description: In the Seraikela-Kharsawan district, close to Jamshedpur, lies Seraikela, a town with a living royal lineage. It is best known for its Chhau dance, one of three recognised UNESCO styles of this martial dance form, and cultural visitors usually make the short drive over from the steel city to see it.

bihar.name: Bihar
bihar.description: Bihar is among the oldest inhabited regions of the country, associated with the Buddha and mighty ancient kingdoms. Its religious circuit includes Bodh Gaya and Nalanda for Buddhist travellers, the pilgrimage city of Gaya, and Patna along the Ganga. Most journeys here begin with a long road trip from Kolkata, a corridor that local drivers know well.

cities.name: Patna
cities.description: Patna, the capital of Bihar, rises along the Ganga and counts itself among the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities. In antiquity it was Pataliputra, seat of the Maurya Empire, and more than 2,500 years of history still show in its monuments and museums. As the state's main hub, it is where most visitors arriving by rail or air pick up cabs for the rest of Bihar.

cities.name: Gaya
cities.description: Gaya is a deeply sacred city, where Hindus perform Pitru Paksha rituals, or Pind Daan, along the Phalgu River. Standing at the town's heart, the Vishnupad Temple anchors its Vaishnava significance, while nearby Bodh Gaya makes Gaya a combined Hindu-Buddhist pilgrimage centre. Its international airport and rail junction bring pilgrims who then travel the final stretches by road.

cities.name: Bodh Gaya
cities.description: Bodh Gaya is the single most sacred site in Buddhism, the place where Siddhartha Gautama gained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi Tree. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the complex draws pilgrims from around the globe to the Mahabodhi Temple Complex, a high point of Indian temple architecture. Visitors usually fly or rail into nearby Gaya and cover the last 13 km by cab.

cities.name: Nalanda
cities.description: Nalanda is the site of the ancient university that ranked among the great seats of learning of the fifth to twelfth centuries. The UNESCO-listed ruins now draw historians, pilgrims, and culture tourists, most of whom reach the site by road from nearby towns.

cities.name: Rajgir
cities.description: Rajgir, once called Rajagriha, sits within a ring of five hills and holds importance for both Buddhists and Jains. It served as the original seat of the Magadha Empire, and today the Vishwa Shanti Stupa and its ropeway are the town's biggest draws, with most attractions linked by short local drives.

cities.name: Muzaffarpur
cities.description: Muzaffarpur is the commercial heart of North Bihar, well known for its Shahi litchis and its busy position on the region's transport network. Places like Ramna Maidan and a number of temples add a historical layer, and the city handles constant traffic of passengers heading deeper into the north.

uttar-pradesh.name: Uttar Pradesh
uttar-pradesh.description: Uttar Pradesh is the country's most populous state and sits at the centre of India's spiritual map. Varanasi, Prayagraj, Mathura, and Ayodhya all fall within its borders, drawing pilgrims from far beyond the region. For travellers arriving from Kolkata, it is a long but popular road journey with plenty of overnight halts.

cities.name: Varanasi
cities.description: Varanasi, also called Kashi or Banaras, claims a place among the oldest living cities on earth and stands as India's spiritual capital. Its Ganga ghats, notably Dashashwamedh and Manikarnika, are legendary, and the evening Ganga Aarti remains a deeply moving ritual. Pilgrims from Bengal form a large share of visitors, and the city's narrow lanes are best left to local drivers while cabs handle the longer routes.

cities.name: Prayagraj
cities.description: Prayagraj, still commonly called Allahabad, is one of Hinduism's holiest cities, built around the Triveni Sangam where the Ganga and Yamuna meet the mythical Saraswati. It hosts the Kumbh Mela, the largest religious gathering anywhere, and sees a steady flow of Bengali pilgrims, who typically arrive by train and use cabs to move between the Sangam, the fort, and Anand Bhawan.
